fields.meta_title: Personal Trainer Landing Page Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a personal trainer landing page from a prompt. See four examples that turn visitors into consults, applications, and booked sessions.
fields.h1: Build a Personal Trainer Landing Page That Books Consults
fields.hero_description: Build a personal trainer landing page that turns visitors into consult requests and saves every lead to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: The Page, and Everything After the Form
fields.features_subheading: A personal trainer landing page has one job: a consult request. Emergent builds the page and what happens to each request.
fields.feature_1:
The page from one description

Describe your offer, the clients you train, and the step you want them to take. Emergent builds the page and its form from that prompt, and changes either one when you prompt again.
fields.feature_2:
Every lead in a table you own

Each request the form takes is saved as a row in a database you own, with the name, goal, preferred days, and date. Sort the rows by goal to see what new clients ask for most.
fields.feature_3:
An alert as soon as a lead arrives

The app emails you or posts in Slack when a consult request comes in, with the client's goal in the message. A reminder follows for any request still unanswered the next morning.
fields.feature_4:
Questions that sort applicants

Ask how many hours a week someone can train, and the app routes the application by the answer. Applicants above your bar go to a review list, and the rest get your self-paced plan.
fields.feature_5:
Your tools connected over their API

The app sends each new lead to the scheduling, email, or CRM tool you already use, as long as that tool has an API. HubSpot and Stripe connect this way, and so do others.
fields.feature_6:
Your own domain, or the code

Host the page on your own domain, which uses credits, or export the page and its database code to your GitHub repository on paid plans and run it on any hosting you choose.

fields.tab_content_1:
A goal arrives attached to every consult request

Marisol Vega books consults for Vega Strength from one page. Its form asks for a goal and preferred days, and nothing else. The page took 31 requests in October. Each new request reaches Marisol by email, and the goal is the first thing she reads.
fields.tab_content_2:
From 4 weekly hours up, applications reach review

Applicants tell Pike Online Coaching how many hours a week they can train. An answer of 4 hours or more sends the application to Dorian Pike's roster review. Anyone under 4 gets an email with the self-paced plan instead. This month, 9 of 23 applicants cleared the bar.
fields.tab_content_3:
Of 70 October leads, 42 came from the bio link

Koa Performance runs the same page behind three links: a social bio, a business listing, and the referral link clients share. Each lead is saved with the link it came from. In October the bio link sent 42 leads, the listing sent 17, and referrals sent 11.
fields.tab_content_4:
The 12-session pack won 9 of 15 requests

Ember Lane Training lists three session packs: 4 sessions for $260, 8 for $480, and 12 for $660. Clients open the page from a text on their phones and tap the pack they want. Of this month's 15 requests, 9 picked the 12-session pack.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Personal Trainer Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Follow seven steps to plan, write, and test a personal trainer landing page that turns visitors into booked consults.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the client you coach best
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Choose one offer for the page
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write the headline around the result
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Show proof a stranger can check
fields.howto_step_1_des: Name one kind of client, such as desk workers who want to deadlift or new runners training for a first race. A page written around one person's goal reads like a plan. A page written for everyone reads like a price list.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Decide the single step a visitor should take: a free consult, an application, or a session pack. Put that step in the headline and on every button. A second offer gets a page of its own and a count of its own.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Lead with what changes for the client, in plain words, such as "Deadlift your body weight by summer." Under it, say who you train, where, and how. Certifications and years of experience belong near the form, where the visitor decides.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Use client results with first names and the weeks they took, with each client's permission. A short clip of you coaching one session shows your cues and your tone better than a paragraph about your training style ever will.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Keep the form to four fields
fields.howto_step_5_des: Ask for a name, an email, a goal, and preferred days. Each extra field is one more place a visitor can stop. Keep questions about injuries and training history for the consult call, where you can ask a follow-up.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Write one prompt with your offer, your form fields, and who gets the alert. Emergent builds the page, the form, and the table each lead lands in. Change a price, a field, or the headline later with another prompt.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test it, then answer the same day
fields.howto_step_7_des: Submit the form from your own phone, check that the alert arrives, and confirm the row appears in your table. Once the page is live, reply to each request on the day it comes in, while the visitor still remembers filling it in.
fields.hero_prompt: Build a personal trainer landing page that saves every signup to a database I own.

faq_plan.q: What is a personal trainer landing page?
faq_plan.a: A personal trainer landing page is a single web page that offers one next step, such as a free consult, and holds the form for it. Visitors arrive from a bio link, an ad, or a referral. Unlike a full website, it leaves out everything that does not lead to that one request.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a personal trainer landing page?
faq_plan.a: Write down the client you train, the offer, and the fields your form needs. Then describe the page to Emergent's AI landing page builder in one prompt. It builds the page with its form and a database that keeps each request, and you change any part of it with another prompt.

faq_plan.q: What sections does a personal trainer landing page need?
faq_plan.a: A headline that names the result and the client it suits, a line on who you train and where, proof such as client results, and one form. Put your certifications near the form. Leave out class schedules and blog posts, which pull the visitor away from the request.

faq_plan.q: Does a trainer at a gym need a separate personal trainer landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you sell your own sessions. A gym's fitness landing page sells memberships and trial passes; yours sells your method and a consult with you. Ask the gym first whether you may take clients directly, then point each page at its own form.

faq_plan.q: Should a personal trainer landing page show prices?
faq_plan.a: Show them when you sell fixed packs, because a visitor who sees the price before the form arrives at the consult knowing the cost. When each plan is custom, show a starting price or say the consult sets it. Hiding every number fills the calendar with calls that end at the price.

faq_plan.q: How many form fields should a personal trainer landing page have?
faq_plan.a: Four are enough for a first request: name, email, goal, and preferred days. Add a phone number only if you plan to call. Save health history and injury questions for the consult or a separate intake form that you send once the client books.

faq_plan.q: Should a personal trainer landing page be about me or the program?
faq_plan.a: Lead with the program and the result a client gets, then introduce yourself next to the proof. Put the outcome first and yourself second. A personal landing page built around your name suits speaking, press, and partnerships, while a trainer page sells sessions.

faq_plan.q: Can a personal trainer landing page screen online coaching applicants?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Ask one question that predicts fit, such as how many hours a week the applicant can train, and set a bar. On a page built with Emergent, the app sorts applications by that answer and sends the ones above the bar to your review list. Change the bar later with one prompt.

faq_plan.q: How do I track which links send leads to a personal trainer landing page?
faq_plan.a: Give each place you share the page its own tagged link, such as one for your bio and one for referrals. Then count leads by tag each month. If Emergent builds the page, each lead is saved with its tag in a database you own, and the monthly count comes from one sorted table.

faq_plan.q: How can a personal trainer landing page capture leads not ready to book?
faq_plan.a: Offer something useful in exchange for an email, such as a four-week beginner plan. That is a lead magnet landing page: one free resource and one short form. Follow up with a short series of emails, and put the consult link in each one.

plan.angle: The results for this keyword are template galleries and design roundups that end at the layout; none of them follows a lead past the button. This page shows four personal trainer landing pages built from a prompt and tracks what each one does with a lead after the form is sent: a consult request that reaches the trainer with the goal attached, an online coaching application routed by weekly training hours, leads tagged by the link they came from, and a session-pack request made from a phone. Siblings stay distinct: fitness covers gyms and studios, coaching covers coaching offers broadly; this page stays on one trainer selling 1:1 training. The FAQ covers the definition, building one, what to include, page versus full website, getting clients from the page, form length, showing prices, a page about the program versus the person, taking applications, and collecting leads from people not ready to buy.
